entities.name: Abbey of St. Victor
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Abbey of Saint-Victor in Paris was a medieval Augustinian abbey founded in 1108 by William of Champeaux, one of the greatest philosophical minds of the early 12th century, which became a leading center of mystical theology and scholarship in medieval Europe. The Victorine school of theology it produced — combining rigorous biblical scholarship with mystical contemplation — influenced Thomas Aquinas, Bonaventure, and the entire scholastic tradition of medieval Christian thought.

William of Champeaux founded Saint-Victor after losing a famous debate to his student Peter Abelard, withdrawing from Paris's cathedral schools to establish a regular monastic community. The school attracted outstanding scholars: Hugh of Saint-Victor (1096-1141), whose Didascalicon created medieval Europe's first systematic classification of the sciences, and Richard of Saint-Victor, whose mystical theology on contemplation influenced Dante and medieval mysticism.

The Victorine synthesis of rational scholarship and mystical contemplation represented a distinctive approach: unlike Peter Abelard's purely dialectical theology or Bernard of Clairvaux's purely affective mysticism, the Victorines sought to integrate both reason and love in the ascent to God. Hugh of Saint-Victor's phrase 'Learn everything; you will find later that nothing is superfluous' became a motto for medieval encyclopedic learning. The abbey survived until the French Revolution, when it was suppressed in 1790.
